sections.h2: What kind of county is Morrison County for a home seller?
sections.html:
Morrison County is a mostly rural, river-and-lake county in central Minnesota, and Little Falls anchors it as seat of government and biggest town. Benton County gave up its northern strip to form it on February 25, 1856. The Mississippi River runs south through the western part, and Camp Ripley Military Reservation fills a big piece of the north-central area. Cass, Crow Wing, Mille Lacs, Benton, Stearns and Todd counties surround it.

Per the QuickFacts table for Morrison County, the July 2025 population estimate is 34,620, with 16,659 housing units across about 1,125 square miles of land. Owners live in 80.6 percent of occupied homes. For 2020 to 2024 the typical owner-occupied home was worth $248,500, typical gross rent was $788 a month, and the median household earned $69,446.

Districts named for the county include Little Falls, Pierz, Royalton and Staples-Motley, plus Swanville, Upsala, Holdingford and others. A buyer comparing a house in Little Falls with one near Pierz is also comparing school districts.

sections.h2: Which offices in Little Falls deal with property tax and deeds?
sections.html:
All three offices share the Government Center at 213 1st Avenue SE, Little Falls, MN 56345. The county switchboard is 320-632-2941, with a toll-free line at 1-866-401-1111, and the front-line county offices post weekday hours from 8 to 4:30.

  • Auditor/Treasurer: sends the tax bills, collects the money and holds the payment counter. Details are on the county's property tax page.
  • Assessor's Office (Land Services): sets estimated market value and classification, and answers value questions at 320-632-0170.
  • Recorder: files deeds and other real estate papers, phone 320-632-0146. Its web page tells visitors the staff cannot advise on law or draft documents, and refers transfer questions to a real estate attorney or an abstract or title firm.

Online, the county directs people to Beacon for maps and tax statements, and to Landshark for recorded documents.

sections.h2: What are the Morrison County tax payment deadlines?
sections.html:
Real property is billed in two installments, due May 15 and October 15, with extra dates for resorts, manufactured homes and farmland. Personal property and severed mineral interest taxes fall due alongside the real property installments. A due date that lands on a Saturday, Sunday or legal holiday slides to the following business day.

Due dates on the Morrison County tax payment page
DateWhat is due
May 15Real property first half, or the full bill when it is $100 or less
May 31Resort property, first half
August 31Manufactured homes, first half, or the full bill when it is $50 or less
October 15Non-agricultural real property, second half
November 15Agricultural real property and manufactured homes, second half

This year November 15 is a Sunday, so the two November payments slide to Monday, November 16. The statewide rule in Minn. Stat. 279.01 uses the same May and October split for bills above $100, and lets agricultural homestead and a few related classes pay the second half through November 15 without penalty.

sections.h2: What payment methods does the Morrison County treasurer accept?
sections.html:
The county lists six channels:

  • Counter: cash or a check made out to Morrison County Auditor/Treasurer, during office hours.
  • Drop box: at Broadway (Highway 27) and 2nd Street SE, emptied every day.
  • Postal mail: addressed to the Auditor/Treasurer at the Government Center. A postmark dated no later than the due date counts as proof the payment was on time.
  • Direct Debit: an enrollment form the county needs 30 days ahead of a due date.
  • Card or eCheck online: American Express, Discover, MasterCard and Visa.
  • Phone: 888-272-9829, then jurisdiction code 3314. Press 1 for personal property, 2 for real estate or 3 for mobile homes.

Fees on electronic payments are 2.59 percent for credit cards, 2.59 percent for debit cards with a $1.10 floor, and $2.15 for an eCheck.

sections.h2: What does a late tax payment cost in Morrison County?
sections.html:
Missing a due date adds 2 percent to a homestead installment and 4 percent to a nonhomestead one. Section 279.01 adds another charge of equal size if the installment is still open on the first day of the next month. After that, 1 percent more accrues each month through December. The ceiling is 8 percent for homestead property and 12 percent for everything else.

One break applies to mailed payments. The treasurer must waive the penalty when the envelope carries a U.S. Postal Service postmark within one business day of the deadline, once per owner. With no readable postmark, the owner may sign an affidavit about the mailing date. The county board can also let the treasurer waive a penalty that would be unjust and unreasonable, so ask the Auditor/Treasurer whether Morrison County has adopted that policy.

sections.h2: What can you do if your Morrison County valuation looks too high?
sections.html:
Gather evidence and talk to the assessor before any hearing. The county's appeals page says the appeal concerns the current estimated market value or classification, which drives next year's taxes. Recent sales of similar homes are the evidence it recommends.

  1. Pull together recent sales of homes like yours.
  2. Phone the Assessor's Office at 320-632-0170 and go over your numbers with a county appraiser.
  3. If that fails, book a slot with your local appeal board, which sits in April.
  4. Still unhappy? Book the special appeal board, which sits in June. It will only hear you after the local board has.
  5. The final route is Minnesota Tax Court.

Hearing dates appear on the valuation notice and in local papers. This year's April and June sessions are over, and the next ones follow the same pattern. A dispute over last year's value cannot go to the assessor. It goes to Tax Court only, with a filing deadline at the end of April in the year the tax is payable.

sections.h2: Does a sale of a Morrison County house change the tax picture?
sections.html:
It does in two ways: the deed has to clear a tax check, and the homestead status resets. When a deed arrives for transfer, Minn. Stat. 272.12 has the auditor look for delinquent tax, and a recorder will refuse the deed that lacks the auditor's note.

Sales above $3,000 also need a value certificate, filed with the auditor under section 272.115. Afterward the assessor drops the homestead label for the next assessment year unless the buyer applies and qualifies. A buyer who files nothing by December 31 is treated as nonhomestead for that year, so the seller's old tax rate does not travel with the house.

If you owe back taxes, inherited the house, or are selling as-is, call the Auditor/Treasurer for the exact payoff, penalties included, before you set a price. Ask whoever handles your closing how the current year's tax will be divided.

faqs.q: Which number reaches the Morrison County assessor?
faqs.a: The assessor's line is 320-632-0170. For payments and balances, use the Government Center switchboard at 320-632-2941 and ask for the Auditor/Treasurer.

faqs.q: What is the final due date for the year's property tax in Morrison County?
faqs.a: October 15 closes out non-agricultural real property. Farmland and manufactured homes run to November 15, which is a Sunday this year, so the effective date is Monday, November 16.

faqs.q: Is paying Morrison County property tax by card possible?
faqs.a: Yes, online or by phone at 888-272-9829 with jurisdiction code 3314. The county lists a 2.59 percent charge on credit cards.

faqs.q: What is the order of Morrison County appeal steps?
faqs.a: Start with the Assessor's Office, then the local board in April, then the special board in June, then Minnesota Tax Court. You need to have used the local board before the special one.

faqs.q: What does the Census report as a typical home value here?
faqs.a: $248,500 for owner-occupied homes in 2020 to 2024. That middle value covers the entire county, so a given house may differ a lot from that middle point.
